one_liner: Bison-style generator that emits pthreads-parallel operator-precedence parsers, up to 5.5x faster than Flex+Bison on ARM.
what_it_does: PAPAGENO takes a Bison-syntax grammar restricted to Floyd's Operator Precedence Grammar (OPG) form, plus a Flex lexer spec, and generates self-contained C source for a multithreaded lexer/parser. Unlike Bison's yyparse()/single-threaded model, the generated code is called as `token_node *parse(int32_t threads, char *file_name)`, splitting the input across threads and building the AST without re-parsing overlapping regions. It is not drop-in: grammars that aren't already OPG must be rewritten (which can be a large transformation, see gotchas).
how_it_is_fast: Exploits the OPG property that the shift/reduce decision between two adjacent terminals depends only on a fixed precedence relation, not on global parse state, so the input can be split into chunks and reduced independently on separate POSIX threads with no wasted re-computation when recombining partial trees. Lexing can likewise be split into an independent parallel pass (test/JSON_parallel_lexer). The README states throughput scales close to linearly with thread count on JSON workloads.
when_to_use: Files large enough for parallelism to amortize thread overhead (paper shows real gains mainly on multi-MB inputs, up to 75MiB JSON / 35MiB Lua)
A grammar that is already an Operator Precedence Grammar, or small enough to convert without exploding the rule set (e.g. arithmetic expressions, JSON)
Batch/offline C parsing on multi-core x86_64 servers or ARM big.LITTLE boards where lexing/parsing is a proven bottleneck
You can vendor and maintain generated C source yourself (Python 2.x generator, no upstream releases since 2015)
when_not_to_use: General LALR(1) or ambiguous/context-free grammars: converting real-world Lua to OPG+Fischer-normal-form blew productions up from 144 to 8547 plus required manual lexer transforms
Small or streaming inputs (KB-scale) — paper reports negligible or negative speedup there from thread migration/NUMA overhead
Anywhere you need Bison's GLR mode or ANTLR-style handling of ambiguous grammars — OPG is a strict LALR(1) subset
Projects needing an actively maintained tool or Python 3 support: last commit 2015-04-20, generator is Python 2.x only, one unresolved GitHub issue
Anywhere a true drop-in Bison/Flex replacement is required — grammar syntax is Bison-like but the generated parser's call signature and build process differ

integration.dependencies: Python 2.x to run the generator; GNU Flex, gcc/clang, Make, and POSIX threads (pthreads) to build the generated parser
integration.min_toolchain: Python 2.x (generator); C with pthreads and GNU Flex for the generated code (paper's own build used gcc 4.9.1, -O3 -march=native)
integration.platforms: x86_64 and ARM (tested on Cortex-A15/A7); requires a POSIX threads implementation (tested on Linux NPTL)
integration.thread_safety: not documented beyond the explicit `parse(threads, file_name)` entry point; no stated guarantees about concurrent parse() calls within one process
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: grammar file uses Bison-like syntax and reuses a normal Flex .l lexer, but the grammar must be an Operator Precedence Grammar and the generated parser has its own call signature instead of yyparse()

gotchas: Generator statically rejects non-OPG grammars (consecutive nonterminals, precedence conflicts) and only prints diagnostics — you must manually restructure the grammar
Real-world grammars can blow up drastically under OPG conversion: Lua went from 144 to 8547 productions in the paper's benchmark
README states terminal/nonterminal names may not start with '_'
Generator itself is Python 2.x only; no indication of a Python 3 port
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick PAPAGENO only when the win you need is multi-core parallelism on a Bison-compatible C grammar that is (or can be forced into) Operator Precedence form; the catalogued siblings (flap, re2c, Pika Parser, winnow, chumsky, MPL/FastParse) are all single-threaded OCaml/Rust tools that get their speedups from fused lexing, code generation, or SIMD/table specialization, not from splitting work across cores, so they don't compete on this axis.
verified_claims_summary: The paper (Barenghi et al., preprint for Science of Computer Programming) benchmarks the PAPAGENO-generated parallel lexer/parser against the authors' own sequential Flex+Bison LALR(1) reference parser, both built with gcc 4.9.1 -O3 -march=native, on a 16-core quad-Opteron 8378 server and a 4x-Cortex-A15 Odroid-XU ARM board, over real-world JSON (2.7KiB-75MiB) and Lua (7KiB-35MiB) inputs. It reports up to 5.5x speedup on the ARM board and a separate maximum 7x speedup for parallel lexing alone vs. sequential Flex (not vs. the full Flex+Bison pipeline); the 16-core server JSON comparison (Fig. 13b) is a 3D plot with no stated exact peak number against Flex+Bison.
status_note: Abandoned: no commits since 2015-04-20, GPL-2.0 licensed, one open GitHub issue and no CI/releases; small enough (a handful of C files plus a Python 2.x code generator) to vendor and maintain yourself if you accept the OPG grammar restriction.
